cim: Inside Slack's Salesforce culture clash: Benioff had ~1 hour with CEO Butterfield pre-deal and didn't use Slack; Butterfield quit after a Davos celebrity panel (Johnny Rodgers/Building Slack)

szoveg_eredeti:
I stood at my reserved desk on the 7th floor of Salesforce’s tower in Vancouver around 9am. There were a pair of monitors mounted to the desk, a power strip, and a chair. Even a mouse. But no keyboard.

The office was mostly empty, with a few people taking calls in phone booths. The Salesforce mascots leered vacantly from omnipresent wall murals. “TechForce is on the 5th floor,” the receptionist told me from behind her face mask when I asked where I could get a keyboard for my desk.

I took the elevator down, badged back in, and found the TechForce area. Except TechForce is only open on Thursdays, I learned from the sign on the desk. It was Tuesday. Nobody seemed to be around.

I arrived that morning with the intention of making the best of our new situation. We’d been encouraged to come back to the office one or two days a week. This was before the Omicron variant of COVID-19 exploded across the world. We were deep into the second year of the pandemic. I was pretty sick of working alone at home and missed my colleagues. Figured it would be good to meet some of the local Salesforce people.

Slack was now fully acquired by Salesforce after a 6-month period of bureaucratic limbo following the purchase announcement. We were in the process of integrating into our new parent company in the fall of 2021. Our beloved Vancouver office remained closed, but the Salesforce office was open. Except TechForce. “Or is it Techforce?” I wondered to myself as I made my way back to the elevators. “Is the Force meant to be capitalized?” There were a lot of forces at Salesforce to be understood.

The cultural gaps between Slack and our new parent were evident everywhere you looked. At Slack our tight-knit culture informed every aspect of our work; how the product was designed, how we communicated with customers, how we ran the service and sold it, and how we coordinated internally.

If you needed help at Slack, you asked in a channel and a human would help. Things got done quickly and courteously. If you needed help with something at Salesforce, you filed a ticket and got an automated email response, and most likely a further automated followup with a link to an internal web page. We understood the practical and logistical differences between our 4,000 person company and our 80,000 person acquirer. Ours was a small town. Theirs was a sprawling city. It was nevertheless a shock for us.

We now had to do mandatory training in Trailhead, Salesforce’s internal learning platform. This involved frequently answering dozens of multiple choice questions. They were easily gamed but gave Salesforce the audit trail they needed to ensure all employees were up to date on internal policies. New job-required quizzes arrived regularly in our inboxes, like spam you couldn’t block. And we had inboxes again. Salesforce used email for internal communication. Coming from a company where our CEO had joked that anyone sending an email for internal communication would be fired, this was an unwelcome reality.

Everyone kept welcoming us to the Ohana. “What the fuck is Ohana?” we wondered. “It’s cultural appropriation is what it is,” others answered bitterly. Salesforce used the Hawaiian word for family as a welcoming umbrella for the company and its employees. They didn’t shy away from using other symbols of Hawaiian culture either: leis and traditional Pacific Islander greetings are common at Salesforce events.

Genuine or not, it rankled many of us Slack people. Slack had certainly developed its own share of corporate cognitive overhead in our 8 years of existence. But what we had was nothing compared to the overbearing weight of the Salesforce monolith.

But these irritating issues were the least of our problems as a newly swallowed subsidiary.

Stewart was brought in under Salesforce’s Bret Taylor, who soon after became co-CEO alongside Marc Benioff. The Slack deal had been made with the working assumption that Bret would be steering as operational CEO, Stewart could focus on making the most of the overlapping capabilities of Slack and Salesforce, and Marc would continue on as the figurehead and founding CEO.

From the get-go Stewart found it difficult to connect with Salesforce’s founder. “I only got about one hour of total facetime with Marc before the deal was announced. My last meeting with him was cut short because McConaughey arrived,” he told me. Matthew McConaughey, that is. Salesforce reportedly pays him $10M annually to be a spokesperson.

Once the deal closed and we began the real work of corporate integration Stewart became deeply frustrated with how poorly run the company seemed to be. Operational efficiency was considered a critical component of Slack’s success. We routinely spent time and energy on maintaining and improving that efficiency across all layers. These efforts were anchored in the experience of Slack’s employees and customers.

Could engineers make meaningful contributions reliably? Did internal events run smoothly? Were product releases coherent and well-considered? Did the cameras in meeting rooms work? Was customer feedback understood and acted upon? Did desks have keyboards? Everyone took accountability for their piece of the puzzle. And everyone felt a deep responsibility to each other to eliminate papercuts, to own and fix chronic issues, and to generally strive to do the best work of our lives.

At Salesforce, Stewart was baffled by the breadth and depth of operational inefficiency. He witnessed executives green-lighting high-priced celebrity appearances while making cuts to things like inter-office employee travel. He saw VPs overhiring by thousands of people, then laying off thousands in subsequent quarters. An annual event for tenured and executive staff named Laulima (Hawaiian for “many hands”) cost millions to fly everyone to Hawaii and put them up in fancy hotels.

Stewart gave feedback on these issues and proposed solutions to Bret and Marc repeatedly, but it seemed to fall on deaf ears.

The practical matters of integration were also going poorly. After the initial restructuring that eliminated duplicate roles, Slack’s core responsibilities were largely left alone. Product, Design and Engineering continued on more or less as they had been before the acquisition. Customer Support stayed within Slack’s control for the time-being. But many of the processes and cultural norms around our teams began to inevitably shift toward Salesforce’s expectations.

This was felt most immediately in Sales. Salesforce makes targeted products for business units and sells to leaders of a single function, usually sales or marketing. Slack makes an inherently cross-functional product that needs actual buy-in from an entire executive team to be successful. Salesforce sells dedicated purpose-built databases for managing information; Slack sells an open canvas for any and every department in a company to collaborate more effectively. The resulting DNA of the two go-to-market teams couldn’t have been more different.

“Salesforce got put onto Slack [the product], but weren’t really using it, especially in Sales. They didn’t understand the product. So they sold the products they understood and were easier to sell vertically. Slack didn’t fit the pattern,” said Cal Henderson. Salesforce account executives weren’t using Slack in their day-to-day beyond direct messages, and had a hard time articulating the value to customers. Many thought adding Slack to a deal created confusion and elongated the sales cycle. And worse, Slack wasn’t a “dashboard metric” for Salesforce reps – there was little incentive to sell.

At Slack, customer engagements were focused on making customers successful, rarely pushing seats or over-promising if it risked a negative experience and slower growth. To be successful, Slack reps had to find internal customer champions and collaborate with them in order to teach decision makers that how their employees communicated could become a competitive advantage.
